tier_reason: bench.vortex.dev is Vortex's own CI dashboard. It compares against Parquet, and the benchmark code is public (benchmarks/compress-bench, random-access-bench, datafusion-bench, duckdb-bench). The page names no hardware or flags. The CI workflows give an AWS instance type (c8gd.metal-24xl), RUSTFLAGS and rustc 1.98.0, but no CPU model, so per precedent this is first-party C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: bench.vortex.dev (live page, build 737386b as of 2026-09-26). Two figures are geomean throughput ratios to Parquet: write throughput 2.97x (1,756 vs 605 MB/s) and scan throughput 30.73x (84.14 vs 3.20 GB/s). The page's other summary ratios are geomean time ratios to the fastest entry (lower is better), not speedups over Parquet. Random access, hot: Vortex 1.15x (1.85 ms) vs Parquet 627.08x (65.32 s), about 545x (derived from page data). Random access, cold: Vortex 1.35x (3.31 ms) vs Parquet 432.76x (67.10 s), about 321x (derived from page data). ClickBench: DataFusion+Vortex 3.99 s vs DataFusion+Parquet 6.08 s, about 1.52x (derived from page data); DuckDB+Vortex 4.65 s vs DuckDB+Parquet 5.45 s, about 1.17x (derived from page data). TPC-H SF1 NVMe: DuckDB+Vortex 450.40 ms vs DuckDB+Parquet 1.51 s, about 3.35x (derived from page data).
corrections.workload: First-party CI benchmark dashboard (bench.vortex.dev) covering write and scan throughput (compress-bench), hot and cold random-access take latency over taxi, feature-vectors, nested-lists and nested-structs datasets, ClickBench, TPC-H SF1/10/100 on NVMe and S3, TPC-DS SF1 and others. Each workload runs with both DataFusion and DuckDB as the query engine, against Parquet, Lance, Arrow IPC and DuckDB native formats.
corrections.hardware: Not stated on the page. The repo's CI workflows (.github/workflows/develop-bench.yml, sql-bench-matrix.yml) run benchmarks on an AWS EC2 c8gd.metal-24xl (ARM64); no CPU model is named.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated on the page. Per the repo's CI workflow: rustc 1.98.0 (rust-toolchain.toml), RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native -C force-frame-pointers=yes', cargo --profile release_debug.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 3,225 stars; LF AI & Data incubation-stage project
corrections.caveats: First-party dashboard whose numbers change with every commit. Most summary 'x' figures are geomean ratios to the fastest entry, not speedups over Parquet, so only the write and scan throughput ratios are direct Parquet comparisons. On the same page, results on S3 are mixed. At TPC-H S3 SF1, DataFusion+Parquet is fastest (6.54 s vs DataFusion+Vortex 8.86 s). At TPC-H S3 SF100, DuckDB+Vortex takes 488.62 s vs 73.45 s for DuckDB+Parquet. The independent ClickHouse/ClickBench results (c6a.4xlarge, sum of best-of-3 over 43 queries, derived from the result JSONs) are also mixed. On 2026-05-11, duckdb-vortex took 40.99 s vs 32.48 s for duckdb-parquet: slower in total because one query is about 20x slower, though it was faster on 26 of 43 queries and about 5% faster by geomean. A 'tuned' duckdb-vortex run on 2026-09-26 took 29.69 s but loaded in 762 s. On 2026-08-20, DataFusion+Vortex took 91.30 s vs 45.57 s for DataFusion+Parquet and was about 1.37x slower by geomean. That contradicts the dashboard's DataFusion ClickBench win, although the engine versions differ (Vortex CLI on DataFusion 53.1.0, Parquet run on 54.0.0). The huge random-access ratios mostly reflect Parquet having no row-level random access.

notes: The record misread the dashboard. Its 1.13x (ClickBench) and 1.32x (TPC-H) figures are ratio-to-fastest scores, not speedups over Parquet, and the Parquet 65.32 s random-access figure is from the hot panel, not a cold/hot mix. I rewrote claimed_speedup with the direct comparisons, marked as derived. I downgraded because the query-engine wins over Parquet are contested by independent ClickBench results, including a new DataFusion+Vortex result that is 2x slower in total. The write and scan throughput wins stand, first-party only.

tier_reason: The bank benchmark page runs PsiTri against RocksDB (plus MDBX, TidesDB and SQLite) using public code (programs/bank_bench.cpp, driven by bench/suites/bank_tpcb.sh; raw logs and machine.json are in docs/data/bank_tpcb/). It states the CPUs (Apple M5 Max; AMD EPYC-Turin 8c/16t 2.4 GHz), the compilers (Clang 17 / Clang 20) and the flags (-O3 -flto=thin / -O3 -flto -march=native).

corrections.workload: TPC-B-style bank-transfer benchmark. Each transfer is one atomic transaction of 5 KV ops (2 reads, 2 updates, 1 insert), with triangular-skew access and a fixed seed. The main runs use 1M accounts, 10M transfer attempts, 100 transfers per commit and sync=none. The PsiTriRocks drop-in comparison is a separate April 2026 EPYC run: 1M accounts, 1M transactions, batch=1, sync=none, write-only and write plus one concurrent reader.
corrections.claimed_speedup: PsiTriRocks (RocksDB-API drop-in) vs RocksDB, April 2026 AMD EPYC-Turin, batch=1: 2.3x write throughput (369,446 vs 157,588 transfers/sec) and 4.9x reader throughput under concurrent writes (1,416,652 vs 289,627 reads/sec). Native PsiTri vs RocksDB in the batch=100 run: 376,691 vs 126,341 transfers/sec on Apple M5 Max, about 2.98x (derived from page data); 163,614 vs 104,102 transfers/sec on AMD EPYC-Turin, about 1.57x (derived from page data).
corrections.hardware: Apple M5 Max, 128 GB unified memory (macOS); AMD EPYC-Turin, 8 cores/16 threads at 2.4 GHz with 121 GB RAM (Vultr cloud VM, Linux 6.17, exact SKU not given)
corrections.caveats: Only 4 GitHub stars and no independent replication. All runs use sync=none (no forced durability). On the AMD EPYC-Turin VM, both MDBX (239,041) and TidesDB (167,093) beat native PsiTri (163,614 transfers/sec), so the win over RocksDB is not a win over every engine tested. The 4.9x figure measures reader throughput under a concurrent writer, not a pure read workload. First-party benchmark.

notes: All record numbers appear on the page and belong to the right rows. I made clarifying fixes: the workload is TPC-B-style, not TATP, and the 2.3x/4.9x figures come from a separate batch=1 run. Metadata checks out: MIT license, 4 stars, last main commit 2026-04-28, active.

tier_reason: Peer-reviewed USENIX FAST'21 paper. Its abstract states the 8.8x throughput and 9.5-58.3% latency gains against vanilla RocksDB v6.5.1, and the code and YCSB harness are public at SpanDB/SpanDB (ycsb/, test binary with dbname=rocksdb|spandb). The paper names the CPU (2x Xeon Gold 6248) but not the compiler version or flags, and the README gives only 'gcc >= 4.8' and CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, so not A.

corrections.hardware: 2x 20-core Intel Xeon Gold 6248, 256 GB DRAM, CentOS 7.7; Intel Optane P4800X, P4510 and P4610 NVMe SSDs, plus S4510 SATA SSDs in 4+1 RAID5, tested as capacity-disk/speed-disk pairs
corrections.claimed_speedup: 'improves RocksDB's throughput by up to 8.8x and reduces its latency by 9.5-58.3%' (FAST'21 abstract). The 8.8x peak comes from the YCSB all-write workload (20M Zipfian writes: 7.6-8.8x across device pairs). The read-heavy YCSB-B/E gains are only 1.03-1.66x in throughput.
corrections.workload: LSM-tree KV store on hybrid storage, SpanDB vs vanilla RocksDB v6.5.1: YCSB all-write, A, B, E and F (Zipfian and uniform) on a 512 GB database, plus LinkBench, across three capacity-disk/speed-disk pairs (S-N2, S-O, N1-O). SpanDB writes its WAL via SPDK to the fast NVMe disk; RocksDB writes WAL to the same disk via ext4.
corrections.caveats: The baseline is RocksDB v6.5.1 (2019). The paper does not state the compiler version or flags. SpanDB needs SPDK, hugepages and a dedicated NVMe device for the WAL, and its gains are largest on write-intensive workloads (read-heavy YCSB-B/E gives 1.03-1.66x). The repo has had no commits since August 2023, so it is an unmaintained research prototype.

notes: I opened the full paper PDF. The numbers match the abstract, and section 5.1 names the hardware and the RocksDB v6.5.1 baseline. Metadata checks out: GPL-2.0, 214 stars, last commit 2023-08-02, abandoned (over 3 years).
